title: Establish and appraise the SMME,s current situation and potential

lessons.title: Gathering information about the SMME
lessons.html:
Why appraise an SMME?

Small, medium and micro enterprises (SMMEs) make up most agricultural businesses in rural South Africa: a broiler house selling live birds, a vegetable co-operative supplying a local Spar, a smallholder piggery, or a contractor doing ploughing with one tractor. Before you can advise or help an SMME access finance or markets, you must understand where it stands today and what it could become. A rushed appraisal leads to poor advice, such as recommending expansion to a business that is already short of cash.

Sources of information

  • Interviews with the owner, partners and key workers. Ask about history, goals, daily operations and problems.
  • Site visit. Walk the farm or premises. Look at the condition of fences, housing, irrigation, vehicles and stores. Note the stock on hand.
  • Records. Request bank statements, sales slips, invoices, stock registers, production records such as egg counts or mortality, and any financial statements.
  • Legal and registration documents. Company or co-operative registration with CIPC, SARS tax status, land tenure documents such as a lease or Permission to Occupy, and any permits or water use authorisation.
  • Market information. Who the customers are, what prices they pay and how reliable demand is.

Many small farmers keep few written records. Do not dismiss them. Help reconstruct figures by asking practical questions: how many bags of feed do you buy a month, at what price; how many birds did you sell at the last batch, at what price per bird. Cross-check answers against bank statements or supplier slips where possible.

Ethics

Explain why you need the information and who will see it. Keep financial records confidential and return original documents. Be respectful: the owner has built the business with their own effort and risk. Your role is to understand, not to judge.

Organise the information in a client file so that it can be analysed systematically in the next step.

lessons.title: Analysing the current situation
lessons.html:
Looking at the business from all angles

Once information is gathered, analyse the SMME in its main functional areas. A simple checklist keeps the appraisal balanced.

AreaQuestions to ask
ProductionAre yields, growth rates or mortality in line with norms? Is equipment adequate and maintained?
MarketingWho buys, at what price, and how secure is the market? Is there a contract?
FinanceIs the business profitable? Does it have enough cash to buy inputs on time? What debt does it carry?
Management and peopleWho makes decisions? Are skills and roles clear? Are labour laws followed?
ComplianceIs the business registered, tax compliant, and holding required permits?

Basic financial analysis

Build a simple income statement for the last season or year: total sales minus direct costs such as feed, seed, fertiliser and casual labour gives the gross margin. Subtract overheads such as electricity, transport, rent and interest to get net profit. Then look at cash flow month by month. Many farm SMMEs are profitable on paper but fail because cash runs out between planting and harvest.

Compare key figures with benchmarks from the commodity organisation, the provincial department or similar farmers. For example, compare feed conversion in a broiler unit or yield per hectare in a cabbage enterprise with local norms.

SWOT analysis

Summarise findings in a SWOT. Strengths and weaknesses are internal: good water supply, skilled owner, poor record keeping, old tractor. Opportunities and threats are external: a new school feeding contract, rising feed prices, stock theft, drought. A good SWOT is specific and supported by evidence, not a list of general statements.

Identify the two or three most critical issues limiting the business. These will guide your appraisal of potential.

lessons.title: Appraising potential and reporting findings
lessons.html:
What could this business become?

Potential is the realistic future the SMME could reach if key constraints are addressed. Appraising potential means testing ideas against the facts of the current situation, the market and the owner's ability and willingness.

Questions to test potential

  • Market: is there proven demand for more product, at a price that covers costs? A letter of intent from a buyer is stronger evidence than general optimism.
  • Resources: is there enough land, water, labour and infrastructure to grow? Is water use authorised under the National Water Act 36 of 1998 if irrigation will increase?
  • Finance: can growth be funded from profits, a loan or a grant, and can the business repay a loan from realistic cash flow?
  • Management capacity: does the owner have the skills and time to run a bigger operation? What support or training would be needed?
  • Risk: what could go wrong, such as disease, drought or price collapse, and how could it be reduced?

Scenario planning

Develop two or three scenarios, for example: stay at current size but improve efficiency; add a second broiler house; or add value through slaughtering and packaging. For each, estimate investment in rand, extra income, extra costs and payback period. Present conservative figures. Often the best first step is improving the existing operation before expanding.

Reporting

Write a clear appraisal report covering: background, current situation by functional area, financial summary, SWOT, critical issues, scenarios and recommendations. Use plain language and tables. Present the report to the owner in person, discuss it and agree on next steps. The owner must accept the findings for any plan to succeed.

Key points

  • Collect information from interviews, site visits, records, legal documents and the market.
  • Analyse production, marketing, finance, management and compliance.
  • Use gross margin, net profit and monthly cash flow to judge financial health.
  • Summarise findings in an evidence-based SWOT and identify critical issues.
  • Test growth scenarios against market, resources, finance, skills and risk.
